title: not fate, not payback
hook: the word everyone borrows, and what it actually says
tomorrow: what your grandmother was actually doing

segments.voice: Yesterday: one truth, many names, and the one that's yours. Six words so far: Ganesha, om, Gayatri, namaste, arti, ishta devata. Today, the seventh.
screen: `GANESHA · OM · GAYATRI · NAMASTE · ARTI · ISHTA DEVATA`

segments.voice: Karma. Someone says it when the car that cut them off gets stopped at the next light. Someone says it when a person who was unkind finally has a bad week. It turns up in song lyrics, on coffee mugs, under photos. Used like that, it means payback: the universe keeping a ledger and settling it on schedule, ideally where you can watch. It's a satisfying idea. It is also not quite what the word means. The older meaning is less about getting even and more about getting made, and it turns the whole thing around to face the one who's using it.
screen: `KARMA.` → `THE CAR AT THE RED LIGHT.` → `PAYBACK?` → `NOT QUITE.`

segments.voice: Karma is the Sanskrit word for action. A deed. Something done. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna points out that no one can stay without acting, even for a moment: breathing, eating, speaking, choosing, all of it is action. So the first thing to know is that karma isn't something that happens to you. It's what you do. The second thing is what action does back. One of the oldest Hindu texts says it like a proverb: as a person acts, so that person becomes. Not: so the person is punished. Becomes. Patience, practiced, turns into a patient person. Sharpness, practiced, turns into a sharp one. A mango seed isn't judged worthy of a mango tree; it grows one because that's what the seed is. The payback version keeps your eyes on other people: did they get what's coming? The older version turns you around: what am I growing with my next word? Hindu teachers also speak of karma across lifetimes, and that's a bigger conversation for later. For today: as you act, so you become.
screen: `KARMA — ACTION, A DEED` · `NO ONE STAYS WITHOUT ACTING` · `AS ONE ACTS, SO ONE BECOMES` · `WHAT AM I GROWING?`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Bring to mind one small thing you did this week: a kind word, a sharp one, a promise kept or skipped. Don't grade it. Just ask what it's growing. Then pick one small action you'd be glad to see grow.
Karma. Action, and what action makes of the one who does it. Not payback. Seventh word: a week's worth.
Your line: what you do, you become. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each. Tomorrow, what your grandmother was actually doing.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers speak of karma as action and its fruit, within this life and across lifetimes; schools of thought differ on how karma works and on how a person is freed from it.

fork.setup: a car cuts you off, then gets stuck at the red light ahead. which thought is closest to the older meaning of karma?
options: that's their action. mine is what I do next.
fork.reveal: karma is action. the Upanishad says as one acts, so one becomes, so the karma in your hands is your own next move.

story.title: the robber's question
story.text: A well-loved telling says the poet Valmiki started out as a robber. One day he tried to rob a wandering sage, who asked him a question: would his family share the weight of what he did? He went home and asked. They said no. What he did was his. Shaken, he changed, and became the poet who would compose the Ramayana.
story.source: a traditional telling of Valmiki's life (later than the Ramayana itself)
